hints: Look at each option and ask, does this increase how often bacteria meet antibiotics, or does it break the pattern of exposure?
Remember resistance spreads by directional selection. A constant selection pressure for one antibiotic favours the resistant allele, so think about what happens if that pressure keeps changing.
walkthrough:
**Spot the real problem - selection pressure**

Antibiotic resistance spreads when antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria but leave resistant mutants alive to reproduce. So any routine, unnecessary or repeated use of the same antibiotic increases selection pressure.

Think: more exposure = more chance for resistance to be selected.

**Compare constant use versus changing use**

If we always use the same antibiotic for an infection, any bacterium with resistance to it has a permanent advantage. If we regularly change the type used, no single resistance allele is favoured for long.

This is like changing the exam rules, so bacteria cannot adapt to just one challenge.

**Pick the practice that lowers the pressure**

Options A, B and D all involve giving antibiotics more often, at high dose, preventatively, or for minor infections the immune system could handle. That increases exposure.

Only option C breaks the consistent selection pressure, so it helps to reduce the spread of resistance.

options.A: High concentrations still expose huge numbers of bacteria, including harmless flora, to strong selection and any survivors will carry resistance.
options.B: Routine preventative use means many people without infection receive antibiotics, greatly increasing unnecessary exposure and selection for resistance.
options.C: Regularly rotating the antibiotic type avoids long term selection pressure for resistance to any one antibiotic, so resistant alleles are not consistently favoured.
options.D: Treating a low level infection that the immune system could clear is unnecessary use and gives bacteria an extra opportunity to evolve resistance.
